vignette: Frank is a 76-year-old widowed cashier of European descent who lives alone in a small apartment he has occupied for over forty years. He came to the clinic at the urging of his daughter, who noticed he had stopped visiting his grandchildren and had become increasingly isolated since a supermarket chain reassigned him to a register near the entrance. He scored 67 on the PCL-5 and described a single, catastrophic event that had reshaped his life: during the final year of the Bosnian War, while visiting his late wife’s hometown, a mortar shell struck the market square fifty yards from where he stood. He remembers the blast wave, the ringing silence, then the sight of bodies and pieces of bodies scattered among overturned vegetable stalls. He had come to believe, in the weeks and months afterward, that the world was a fundamentally dangerous place—a place where safety was an illusion. What frightened him most was not the memory of the explosion itself, but the conviction that he was no longer capable of doing the things that had defined him: driving his car, walking through a crowded store, trusting that the ground beneath his feet would not suddenly erupt. He had lost his faith in people, life, or a higher power; he felt, as he put it, that the universe had shown him its true face, and it was indifferent to suffering. These negative appraisals colored every recollection. When he tried to remember the market square, the images came back as vivid pictures—the red of a crushed tomato, the angle of a child’s shoe—but he felt completely numb, as if it had happened to a stranger. Yet at other times, the memory seized him with such force that he felt it was happening right now: the heat, the smell of cordite, the wet cobblestones. Each time this happened, it reinforced his belief that he was broken, that the world could never be safe, and that he was no longer the man he had been. Over the months, Frank developed a set of strategies to manage this overwhelming internal state. He stopped driving entirely—both as a driver and as a passenger—because the sight of an oncoming vehicle or a sudden brake light could trigger a flashback. He pushed away positive emotions, because they felt unsafe; a moment of laughter with a customer would leave him disoriented and watchful, as if joy itself was a trap. He also found himself thinking endlessly about why the event had happened to him, circling the same unanswerable questions for hours. These strategies, while intended to protect him, had the paradoxical effect of making his memories more intrusive. The more he avoided driving, the more the images of the market square surfaced when he sat in a bus or a taxi. The more he suppressed positive feelings, the more the numb, dissociated quality of his recall deepened. His hypervigilance grew steadily worse. He was superalert and watchful on guard, scanning every customer who approached his register for signs of threat. He watched other people closely for signs that they might harm him, and he had difficulty falling asleep because he needed to stay alert, his ears tuned to every creak of the building. This constant threat monitoring, in turn, fed his negative appraisals: the world was dangerous, he was no longer capable, and he had lost his faith. It also strengthened his reliance on maladaptive strategies—he avoided driving more strictly, pushed away happiness more forcefully, and spent longer hours in his ruminative loop. The cycle tightened. At work, the front entrance became a trigger: every time a customer walked through the automatic doors, Frank’s heart rate spiked, and the images of the market square flooded back. He began taking longer breaks, then asked to be moved to a register in the back of the store, but the company refused. He stopped visiting his daughter’s home because the twenty-minute drive required him to be a passenger in her car. He stopped going to the grocery store, relying on delivery services. He stopped answering the phone. What finally brought him to seek help was a moment in the break room when a coworker laughed at a joke, and Frank felt such a surge of dread that he locked himself in the bathroom for an hour. He was most afraid that he would never feel safe again—that the world would always be a place where a mortar shell could fall, and that he would spend the rest of his life watching for it. But he was also, beneath that, hoping that someone could show him how to stop the loop.
